In your business plan, it's a good idea to identify the market for your good/service that you will be selling. This includes some analysis of how much you plan to price your products/services, how much your products/services cost for you in terms of time and materials, what sort of competition exists (and what their typical prices are), how big the market is (demand), and an overview of your marketing strategy including expected advertising expenses and what sort of conversion rates you need for the marketing to be viable.

If your business plan is able to demonstrate that you will be able to generate a decent profit, that gives you and your investors (bank) confidence that the business will succeed and is worthy of a loan. Another benefit is that your models can be used to help you identify the ideal amount of money to be loaned. You don't want to take too much (because you're paying back interest), but you definitely don't want to take too little and get caught flat-footed. Some businesses are more naturally scalable than others. If yours is easy to scale (handle any amount of customers), it could even turn out to make sense to take out more money and invest in getting more employees/marketing. Then again, it's probably simpler and less risky to hold off on doing that. You can still go for a "Round 2" of funding after your business is founded, operating normally, and making its payments on the initial loan.
